title: Society and politician gigs paying well
summary: He describes paying private gigs for politicians, the country club, and Peter Williams.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: When was the last time you played like a regular music? A regular guy? You mean like working at certain numbers and nights every week?

Well I worked down there, at one time I worked in Alvin's Place, and I was playing I worked at 600 Club in Boydman Street, I had a group down there for about five weeks. Al Hurt was at the Blue Note in Chicago, and I worked down there. Where was that?
That was the last time you were.

What I mean, you asked me about a job that I worked on, well I'm telling you, you understand. You understand what I'm saying? Well see, I could have worked on a lot of jobs, but to tell you, it didn't pay. You see what I'm talking about? Because I could do better, but what I was doing, see because Congressman Boggs and all them kind of people, they paid me $10 to $15 an hour just to walk around with that guitar and play. You understand? You understand? 1729 Poist Street when they'd be in town and all them people, you understand? All them big politicians. I can play anything and when they get half high, just play, just wear a doctor, all them people back there in metric. And I had another one, this woman there back there at the country club, what's her name again, I was supposed to play from one to, with Charlotte, Charlotte's job, piano player.
Olivier Charlotte. Yeah. I was supposed to play from eleven o'clock to one. You know when we left there? And through me. Nine at night.

Because all them people recognized me, knew me, and Peter Williams, he used to be a drum player, he was the footman back there. He, you know, tuxed in. What happened to him? I mean he looked back, he looked back to Gravity Street somewhere back there by the old jail. Well he was the footman or he was the butler back there, something like that. And I played back. You see, all them big shots and top of the, I guess a lot of like Connors and Bob's daughters, brothers and people, all them kind of people out there on State Street and all of them, when they have something like that, when a lot of time they used to get out of the French band, different things like that, when they wanted somebody to entertain them, it was simple.
But they don't drink do they?

Well they don't swim in it. Do they drink? You mean I don't drink. Yeah you don't drink. When I'm there all I'm drinking is lemon and water. You keep the pipes free. Because I'm watching them hours. I ain't worried about, I get all the liquor I want. I ain't worried about that. You understand? And we have to do they drink. You can't buy what they drink. As much as they drink, sure they drink. We've got butlers and waiters. I played with a band back in metric from eight to twelve. And they hired me to play the balance till twelve to seventy the next morning. I made about four hundred dollars with tips and everything. Did you ever hear Buddy Petit or Chris Kelly or any of those bands? Well I was coming up when I was kind of young. But I wasn't playing no music. But I heard them. But I didn't know too much about music. I made about $400 with Tipton. Did you ever hear Buddy Petit or Chris Kelly or any of those bands? Well I was coming up when I was kind of young, but I wasn't playing no music, but I heard them, but I didn't know too much about music then.
Yeah, I was wondering about Peter Williams, who he played with.
Peter Williams was a drum player or something like Adler. Holding the drums off.
